title: Climate Adaptation and Polycrisis Resilience
subtitle: A Systemic Vulnerability-Reduction Research Agenda for 2026–2035
description: Why climate adaptation should be treated as systemic vulnerability reduction, with seven research pillars, regional priorities and a ten-point agenda for 2026–2035.
contribution: Develops climate adaptation as a pillar of Polycrisis Resilience: seven research pillars, a map of interventions to interconnected vulnerabilities, six strategic research questions, regional priorities, ten priorities for 2026–2035 and a proposed Adaptation Resilience Dividend.
abstract: Climate change interacts with poverty, food insecurity, water scarcity, public-health risk, infrastructure deficits, economic instability, migration and geopolitical pressure, and where adaptive capacity is thin these interactions can amplify vulnerabilities into cascading crises. This paper asks what changes if climate adaptation is planned as a system rather than as a set of separate sector projects, and proposes that effective adaptation strengthens the underlying systems that let societies withstand, absorb and respond to interconnected disruptions.

It organizes the field into seven research pillars (climate-resilient infrastructure; agricultural and food-system adaptation; water security; public health and heat adaptation; ecosystem-based adaptation; energy resilience and technological diffusion; and institutional and economic adaptive capacity), maps interventions to the interconnected vulnerabilities they address, and sets out six strategic research questions, a financing analysis centred on avoiding unsustainable debt, regional priorities for five regions, and ten research priorities for 2026–2035 in three phases.

It proposes nine outcome families for measuring success and a candidate measure, the Adaptation Resilience Dividend, to be tested, and sets out the risks of maladaptation, equity gaps and the limits to adaptation. All frameworks are proposals open to testing; illustrative scores and projections are labelled as such and are not forecasts.
coreProposition: Climate adaptation should be understood as a systemic vulnerability-reduction strategy rather than a narrowly defined environmental intervention: effective adaptation strengthens the underlying systems that enable societies to withstand, absorb and respond to interconnected disruptions.

keyFindings.title: Adaptation is a vulnerability problem, not only a hazard problem.
keyFindings.text: Risk combines hazard, exposure and vulnerability; the last two are shaped by development choices and are where policy has most influence.

keyFindings.title: Seven pillars cover the main channels of risk.
keyFindings.text: Infrastructure, food, water, health and heat, ecosystems, energy and institutions each reduce several vulnerabilities at once, and none works well alone.

keyFindings.title: Adaptation can interrupt cascades.
keyFindings.text: The same intervention often addresses several interconnected vulnerabilities, for example water infrastructure that reduces drought exposure, protects health and stabilizes farm income.

keyFindings.title: Finance, capacity and sequencing are the binding constraints.
keyFindings.text: International public adaptation finance was about $26 billion in 2023 against estimated needs of $310 to $365 billion a year by 2035 (UNEP, 2025).

keyFindings.title: Priorities differ by region.
keyFindings.text: Sub-Saharan Africa needs agriculture, water and energy; South Asia heat, flooding and food systems; Southeast Asia coastal and urban flood protection; Latin America water and biodiversity; small island states coastal protection and economic resilience.

keyFindings.title: Outcomes, not projects, should be measured.
keyFindings.text: Nine outcome families and a proposed Adaptation Resilience Dividend (illustrative, grade D) would add avoided losses and co-benefits while removing double-counting.

bottomLine: The task is not to eliminate climate risk, which is not possible, but to ensure that when shocks come, systems bend rather than break and the most exposed are not left to face them alone.

glossary.definition: Adjustment to actual or expected climate and its effects in order to moderate harm or exploit opportunity.
Proposed measure of the net value of losses avoided and well-being gained through adaptation, with explicit rules against double-counting (grade D).
The ability of systems, institutions and people to adjust to potential damage, take advantage of opportunities or respond to consequences.
In insurance, the mismatch between a payout trigger (such as rainfall) and the loss a policyholder actually suffers.
A sequence in which failure in one system transmits to others, amplifying harm beyond the original shock.
H Heuristics concept on sequencing: risk sets the deadline, development sets the pace.
Use of biodiversity and ecosystem services as part of an overall adaptation strategy.
The presence of people, livelihoods, infrastructure and assets in places that could be adversely affected.
A potentially damaging physical event or trend, such as heat, flood, drought or storm.
H Heuristics concept that values lives and capital protected, using value-of-statistical-life accounting.
Human Vulnerability Reduction Economics: the H Heuristics concept on who is exposed, across four exposure arenas.
The final step in an early-warning system, in which a warning reaches and is acted on by the people at risk.
Harm from climate impacts that adaptation cannot or does not prevent, and the arrangements to address it.
Action that increases rather than reduces vulnerability, for the actor, for others or for the future.
A measure that delivers net benefits under all plausible climate futures.
A set of interconnected crises whose combined effect exceeds the sum of their separate effects.
Capacity of people, communities, economies, institutions and systems to anticipate, withstand, adapt to, recover from and reduce cascading and compounding crises.
H Heuristics concept that investing before disasters costs less than paying after them.
Matching different instruments (reduction, reserves, contingent finance, insurance) to events of different frequency and severity.
H Heuristics concept on closing the gap between richer and developing economies without past growth's damage.
The propensity or predisposition to be adversely affected, including sensitivity and lack of capacity to cope and adapt.
